Persian polymath, physician, and philosopher of the Islamic world, known in Arabic as Ibn Sina. A seminal figure of the [[Islamic Golden Age]], he served in the courts of various Iranian rulers and influenced medieval European medical and Scholastic thought. His best-known works are *[[The Book of Healing]]*, a philosophical and scientific encyclopedia, and *[[The Canon of Medicine]]*, which became a standard text at many medieval European universities and remained in use as late as 1650.

Avicenna was born in the village of Afshana, near the Samanid capital of Bukhara, to a Persian family; his father, a Samanid official, came from Balkh in [[Bactria]]. He was educated in Bukhara and had memorized the entire [[Quran]] by age 10. He then studied arithmetic with an Indian greengrocer, fiqh with the Hanafi jurist Ismail al-Zahid, and philosophy with al-Natili, with whom he read Porphyry's *Isagoge*. After he had read Ptolemy's *Almagest* and *[[Euclid's Elements]]*, al-Natili told him to continue alone, and by 18 he was well educated in Greek sciences. At 17 he became physician to the Samanid ruler Nuh II. He later moved to Gurganj, the capital of Khwarazm, where he met scholars including [[Al-Biruni]].

Of the 450 works he is believed to have written, around 240 survive, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine. He wrote mostly in Arabic but also produced several key works in Persian, and his poetry appears in both languages. His philosophy belonged to the Peripatetic school derived from Aristotelianism, and he distinguished essence from existence and argued for a necessary existent. His method combined empirical observation, philosophical reasoning, and logical analysis, most visibly in the *Canon*. His thought influenced [[Thomas Aquinas]] and Scholasticism.

Nahuatl-speaking peoples and Mesoamerican civilization of central Mexico, c. 1300–1521. The term is often restricted to the Mexica of Tenochtitlan but is also used for the Nahua peoples of central Mexico in general. It was not an endonym; some scholars have criticized it and proposed alternatives such as Culhua-Mexica.

Aztec society was organized into city-states (altepetl), divided between nobility (pipiltin) and commoners (macehualtin), and shared Mesoamerican traits including [[Maize]] cultivation, a pantheon, and a calendric system. The Mexica were late arrivals to the Valley of Mexico and founded [[Tenochtitlan]] on islets in Lake Texcoco, around 1325 by one account. In 1427 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan formed the Triple Alliance, or [[Aztec Empire]], to defeat the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco. Texcoco and Tlacopan soon became junior partners. The empire was never a territorial state held by garrisons: it dominated client city-states by installing friendly rulers, arranging marriage alliances, and extracting taxes, and it extended its reach through trade and conquest. Religion included human [[Sacrifice]]; excavations at the Templo Mayor have uncovered skull racks.

The empire reached its greatest extent in 1519, when Spanish forces led by [[Hernán Cortés]] arrived. Cortés allied with city-states hostile to the Mexica, and epidemics including [[Smallpox]] struck the population. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521 with the capture of the emperor Cuauhtémoc, and the Spanish founded [[Mexico City]] on its ruins, ruling through local nobles. Aztec history is known from archaeology, Indigenous writings, Spanish eyewitness accounts, and works such as the bilingual *Florentine Codex*, compiled by the friar Bernardino de Sahagún with Aztec informants.

Domain of mostly single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms, typically a few micrometres long. Bacteria were among the first life forms on Earth, appearing about 4 billion years ago, and for about 3 billion years they and [[Archaea]] were the dominant forms of life. They inhabit nearly every habitat, including air, [[Soil]], water, acidic [[Hot spring|hot springs]], radioactive waste, and the deep biosphere of [[Earth's crust]].

Bacterial cells have no nucleus and rarely contain membrane-bound organelles; their DNA usually forms a circular chromosome. Most reproduce by binary fission. Shapes include spheres, rods, and spirals, and cell-wall structure divides them into Gram-positive and Gram-negative types. The word comes from the Greek for staff or cane, because the first ones discovered were rod-shaped. Once classed as plants, bacteria were recognized in the 1990s as one of two very different prokaryotic groups, the other being archaea. Although an estimated 43,000 species have been named, most have never been studied; 90% of research focuses on less than 1% of species.

Bacteria are essential to the nutrient cycle, recycling nutrients, fixing atmospheric nitrogen, and driving decomposition. Near [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]], extremophile bacteria convert compounds such as hydrogen sulphide and [[Methane]] into energy. Eukaryotic cells arose when ancient bacteria entered endosymbiotic associations with their ancestors, giving rise to mitochondria and, later, chloroplasts. Humans carry approximately 10¹³ to 10¹⁴ bacteria, mostly in the gut; most are harmless or beneficial. Pathogenic species cause [[Cholera]], syphilis, anthrax, leprosy, [[Tuberculosis]], tetanus, and bubonic plague. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, but their use in farming has made resistance a growing problem. Bacteria also serve in sewage treatment, cheese and yogurt fermentation, mining of gold, palladium, and copper, and biotechnology.

Capital and largest city of Thailand (pop., 2024: 9.1 million), in the Chao Phraya River delta in central Thailand. Known in Thai as Krung Thep Maha Nakhon, it covers 1,568.7 sq km. The surrounding Bangkok Metropolitan Region has over 17.4 million people (2021 estimate), about 25% of Thailand's population, making Bangkok a [[Megacity|megacity]] that dwarfs the country's other urban centres.

The site began as a village and customs outpost under Ayutthaya in the early 15th century. After Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, King Taksin made it his capital, and in 1782 King Phutthayotfa Chulalok ([[Rama I]]) moved the capital to Rattanakosin Island on the east bank; the City Pillar was erected there on April 21, 1782. Under Mongkut and [[Chulalongkorn]] in the late 19th century the city saw the introduction of the steam engine, the printing press, railways, utilities, formal education, and healthcare. Absolute monarchy was abolished in 1932, and the city has since been the stage for coups, uprisings, and protests, notably in 1973, 1976, 1992, 2006–13, and 2020. Bangkok was bombed by the Allies in [[World War II]], and rapid growth followed with U.S. aid and investment.

The Asian investment boom of the 1980s and 1990s drew regional corporate headquarters, and the city is now a regional centre of finance, business, health care, and the arts. Landmarks include the Grand Palace and the temples Wat Arun and Wat Pho; it is also known for street life and its [[Red-light district|red-light districts]]. Rapid growth with little [[Urban planning|planning]] left inadequate roads and chronic congestion, which caused severe [[Air pollution]] in the 1990s. The city now operates 10 urban rail lines, but congestion persists.

Country in South Asia, on the Bay of Bengal. Officially the People's Republic of Bangladesh, it has a population of almost 180 million in 148,461 sq km, making it the eighth most populous country and one of the most densely populated. [[Dhaka]] is the capital and largest city; Chittagong is the second-largest city and busiest port.

The territory was ruled by successive Hindu and Buddhist dynasties, including the [[Maurya Empire]] and [[Gupta Empire]], before the Muslim conquest of 1204. It later fell under the Bengal Sultanate and the [[Mughal Empire]], whose largest subdivision, Bengal, became a commercial centre known for textiles. The Battle of Plassey in 1757 began nearly two centuries of British rule. After the [[Partition of India]] in 1947, the region became East Pakistan, the eastern wing of Pakistan.

After the Pakistani military launched Operation Searchlight, the [[Bangladesh Liberation War]] began; Bangladesh became sovereign on December 16, 1971, after Pakistani forces had carried out what is known as the Bangladesh genocide, with estimates of deaths up to three million. [[Sheikh Mujibur Rahman]] led the country until his assassination in 1975. Hussain Muhammad Ershad ruled as dictator through the 1980s. Since parliamentary democracy was restored in 1991, politics has been dominated by the Awami League under Sheikh Hasina and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party under Khaleda Zia. Hasina was ousted by a mass uprising in 2024, and an interim administration governed until the February 2026 election, which the Nationalist Party won.

Bangladesh is a unitary parliamentary republic with eight divisions and 64 districts. It hosts the world's largest mangrove forest and is exposed to floods, cyclones, and [[Climate change]].

Financial institution that accepts deposits from the public and makes loans. Banks create demand deposits while lending, either directly or through capital markets and acting as payment agents through checking accounts and transfers. Banks issue new [[Money]] when they make loans.

Banks play an important role in financial stability and national economies, so most countries regulate them heavily. Most countries use fractional-reserve banking, under which banks hold liquid assets equal to only a portion of their current liabilities. Banks are also generally subject to minimum capital requirements under an international set of standards, the [[Basel]] Accords.

Banks borrow by accepting deposits and by issuing debt securities such as banknotes and [[Bond (finance)|bonds]]. They lend through advances on current accounts, installment loans, and investment in marketable debt securities. Activities range from personal, corporate, and private banking to investment banking, trade finance, and consumer finance, and customers reach them through branches, ATMs, and online and mobile banking. Revenue comes mainly from the spread between the [[Interest (economics)|interest]] paid on deposits and charged on loans, with fees and financial advice providing a more stable income stream.

Early practices of credit and lending date to the ancient world; one account places temple-based safekeeping and lending in Mesopotamia around 2000 BC. Banking in its modern sense evolved in the 14th century in the cities of [[Renaissance]] Italy, where banking dynasties such as the Medicis and Fuggers played a central role. The Bank of Amsterdam was founded in 1609 and the Bank of England in 1694. The oldest existing retail bank is Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena (founded in 1472), and the oldest existing merchant bank is Berenberg Bank (founded in 1590).

Chemical substance that reacts with acids. Three definitions are in common use, all agreeing that bases react with [[Acid|acids]].

In 1884 [[Svante Arrhenius]] proposed that a base dissociates in aqueous solution to form hydroxide ions (OH⁻), which combine with hydrogen ions from acids to form water. A base was therefore a metal hydroxide such as NaOH or Ca(OH)₂. In the more general Brønsted–Lowry theory (1923), a base is a substance that accepts hydrogen cations (H⁺), that is, [[Proton|protons]]. This includes aqueous hydroxides and other bases such as [[Ammonia]] (NH₃) and its organic derivatives, the [[Amine|amines]]. In Lewis theory, a base is an electron-pair donor; this is more general still, since the Lewis acid need not be a proton and can be a molecule such as boron trifluoride (BF₃).

In water, bases yield solutions with a pH above 7.0 at standard conditions. A soluble base that releases OH⁻ ions quantitatively is called an alkali. Basic solutions feel slippery, taste bitter, turn red litmus paper blue, and conduct electricity. Concentrated or strong bases are caustic to organic matter and react violently with acids. Strong bases such as [[Sodium hydroxide]] ionize completely in water, while weak bases ionize only partially. A reaction between aqueous solutions of an acid and a base is called neutralization and produces water and a [[Salt (chemistry)|salt]].

The term base was first used in 1717 by Louis Lémery as a synonym for the Paracelsian term matrix. Its modern meaning is usually attributed to G.-F. Rouelle, who in 1754 defined a neutral salt as the product of an acid with any substance capable of serving as a base for it.

Seed of plants in many genera of the legume family (Fabaceae), used as a vegetable for human consumption or as animal feed. Beans are sold fresh or dried (a pulse). Most are summer crops, with peas the exception. As [[Legume|legumes]], the plants fix nitrogen and so need less fertilizer than most plants, and their seeds have a high protein content. India is the largest producer.

Beans have been cultivated since the seventh millennium BC in Thailand, and since the second millennium BC in Europe and Peru. Beans were deposited with the dead in [[Ancient Egypt]]. Cowpeas, which include black-eyed peas, were domesticated in sub-Saharan Africa in the second millennium BC. The most widely eaten species is the common bean, *Phaseolus vulgaris*, native to the Americas and domesticated about 8,000 years ago. Most beans eaten today belong to *Phaseolus*, and five kinds were domesticated by pre-Columbian peoples; the common bean, [[Lima bean|lima and sieva beans]], tepary, scarlet runner, and polyanthus beans. [[Christopher Columbus]] was the first European to encounter them, probably in the Bahamas. Pre-Columbian peoples grew beans with [[Maize]] and squash in the Three Sisters method of companion planting.

Beans are cooked in soups, stews, salads, and curries. Some are processed into tofu or fermented into tempeh, and the unripe pods of some varieties are eaten as green beans. Many ripe beans contain toxins such as phytohaemagglutinin and must be cooked to be safe, and many contain oligosaccharides that cause flatulence. Plant breeding that favors a few productive varieties threatens bean diversity; the Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds more than 40,000 accessions of *Phaseolus* beans (2023).

Quality of objects that makes them pleasurable to perceive, and a central subject of [[Aesthetics]]. Landscapes, sunsets, people, and works of art are typical examples. As a positive aesthetic value, beauty is contrasted with ugliness, and it is often listed with [[Truth]] and goodness as one of three fundamental concepts of human understanding.

A central difficulty is that beauty seems both objective and subjective. It is treated as a property of things, yet it depends on the emotional response of observers, hence the saying that it is in the eye of the beholder. Objectivists hold that beauty is a mind-independent feature of things; subjectivists deny this, an approach influenced by [[John Locke]]'s distinction between primary and secondary qualities. Judgments of beauty rest on feeling yet claim universal correctness, a tension called the antinomy of taste. [[David Hume]] suggested that the sense of taste can be trained and that the verdicts of experts coincide in the long run, implying that standards of beauty are intersubjective. [[Immanuel Kant]] distinguished free beauty from adherent beauty, which depends on a thing's conception or function.

Classical conceptions, associated with [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]], define beauty by proportion, harmony, and the integration of parts into a whole. Hedonist conceptions see beauty as bound to pleasure, so that a thing is beautiful if it causes disinterested pleasure. Others define it through value, a loving attitude, or function. Empirical research has linked facial attractiveness to features such as symmetry, averageness, and signs of health, and some researchers read these as evolved cues of reproductive fitness. Researchers dispute how far biology and culture each shape standards of beauty.

Capital city of China (pop., more than 21.8 million), the world's most populous national capital and, after Shanghai, China's second-largest city by urban area. Formerly romanized as Peking, it lies in northern China on the [[North China Plain]] and is a provincial-level municipality of 16 districts, covering 16,410.54 sq km and mostly surrounded by Hebei province. It neighbors Tianjin to the southeast.

Human habitation is ancient: *Homo erectus* fossils at Zhoukoudian date to 230,000–250,000 years ago. The name Beijing, meaning Northern Capital, was applied in 1403 under the [[Ming dynasty]] to distinguish it from Nanjing, the Southern Capital. The city has been the country's political center for most of the past eight centuries, having been established as a capital by the Jin dynasty in 1151 and developed under the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. It is the seat of the [[Chinese Communist Party]] and central government, whose handling of dissent, notably the 1989 [[Tiananmen Square]] crackdown, has drawn international criticism.

The city has eight [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites, among them the [[Forbidden City]], the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, and the Ming Tombs, alongside traditional hutong alleys and siheyuan courtyard houses. It hosts 176 foreign embassies and the headquarters of most of China's largest state-owned companies. [[Tsinghua University]] and [[Peking University]] are among its leading institutions, and the Zhongguancun area is a center of technology and entrepreneurship. Beijing Capital International Airport was Asia's busiest from 2009 to 2019, and Beijing Daxing International Airport has the largest single-structure airport terminal in the world. Beijing hosted the 2008 Summer Olympics and in 2022 became the first city to host both Summer and Winter Olympics.
